first.rationale: The objective is sustainable long-term qualified revenue, not raw acquisition, so the two inherited beliefs most likely to swing this decision are also the two whose evidence is weakest against that objective. memory_73 (promotional pricing) is the intuitive answer to the competitor's entry pricing and would be the most costly mistake: its recorded support is 'acquisition and revenue lift', which is a short-horizon, discount-driven proxy with no stated retention, margin, or revenue-quality follow-through. Price-matching a competitor's entry price can import exactly the price-sensitive, low-LTV cohort that degrades qualified revenue while appearing to win the quarter, and pricing moves are hard to reverse once signalled to the market. That combination of high consequence and insufficient support for the stated objective makes it the top verification priority even though it is not my intended action. memory_86 (shortening onboarding) is my intended direction and is the closest match to the observed internal decline (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6% QoQ), but its support is also proxy-level: completion rates and time-to-value, plus 'early product adoption'. None of that establishes a link to qualified revenue, so I want the original record to check whether the lift persisted and whether it was measured on accounts that later converted. I did not spend the second pull on memory_31, memory_57, or memory_44 because they are less decision-critical here: memory_31 points the same direction as memory_86, referral incentives do not address a top-of-funnel activation decline, and enterprise sales-assist does not address the SMB segment under attack. I do flag a downstream value risk on the signup-simplification variant of this direction: cutting required fields (memory_31) raises activation by removing the very fields used to qualify and route leads, so an 'activation win' can arrive alongside a decline in lead quality and thus in qualified revenue. If verification shows memory_86 rests only on completion-rate proxies, I will scope the test to reducing friction in onboarding steps rather than stripping qualifying fields, and instrument it on downstream qualified pipeline and 30/60-day retention rather than completion alone. All of this is provisional on the two archive pulls; if memory_73's record turns out to include durable retention and margin evidence and memory_86's does not survive scrutiny, I would reconsider a tightly bounded, time-boxed pricing test instead. Scale is a standard experiment with qualified-revenue and retention guardrails, not a broad rollout, since the causal link from onboarding completion to sustainable revenue is still unverified.

final.rationale: The two pulls resolved the decision in the direction I suspected but could not have asserted without them. exp_73 shows targeted discounting is a trap against the stated objective: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% look like exactly the answer to the competitor's entry pricing, but 30-day retention -12% means the acquired cohort does not survive the first renewal cycle, and the source record explicitly warns against generalizing discounting as sustainable growth. The consolidated memory_73 summary had compressed away the retention harm entirely, which is precisely the failure mode that would have made promotional_pricing the tempting and wrong call this week. Promotional pricing is therefore ruled out on the merits, not merely deprioritized. exp_86 came back confirmed with the link I was missing: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. That retention figure is what upgrades onboarding from a proxy-level belief to one that plausibly reaches sustainable qualified revenue, and it matches the observed internal decline (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6% QoQ). Shortening onboarding also addresses the real internal cause rather than reacting to the competitor's price signal, which is the more durable response to segment pressure. I am running simplify_onboarding as a standard experiment with guardrails, not a broad rollout. Two residual uncertainties keep me off broad rollout. First, exp_86 measured retention at 30 days; sustainable qualified revenue lives at the renewal horizon, so a 30-day lift is encouraging but not conclusive, and I will instrument downstream qualified pipeline plus 60/90-day retention rather than declaring victory on completion rate. Second, memory_31 remains unverified and I spent my budget elsewhere. It recommends cutting required signup fields, which is a materially different intervention from shortening the onboarding flow: removing fields raises activation partly by deleting the data used to qualify and route leads, so it can manufacture an activation win while quietly degrading lead quality and qualified revenue. I am therefore scoping this to reducing friction within onboarding steps as tested in exp_86, and explicitly not stripping qualifying fields, since that variant carries an unverified downstream value risk of the same shape exp_73 just demonstrated. Enterprise_sales_assist and referral_incentive stay unused this week: neither addresses the SMB activation and onboarding decline that the data actually points at.
